newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary to build 500 mln ECU subway in Budapest.
newsitem.headline: Hungary to build 500 mln ECU subway in Budapest.

text.p: Hungary said on Friday it will build a 514 million ECU ($590 million) subway line in Budapest, the first new line in over two decades.
Prime Minister Gyula Horn, announcing the project, called it the country's "biggest construction project in decades."

"The government has made a final decision: the subway shall be built between (the southwestern part of Budapest and the city centre)," he told a news conference, adding that construction will begin in 1998 and end in 2002.

Budapest Mayor Gabor Demszky said the new line will greatly relieve congestion and pollution by cutting car and bus traffic in the Hungarian capital, the second-biggest city in Central Europe behind Berlin with a metropolitan area population of 2.6 million people.
Budapest built a bypass and a bridge to connect the rapidly growing southwestern section of the city with roads leading to southern and eastern Hungary.
But geography forces traffic heading downtown to go through a narrow strip of land between the Danube river and several steep hills, and traffic jams are a daily occurrence.
To finance the subway line, Horn said that Hungary hopes to get a 200 million ECU long-term loan from the EU's European Investment Bank.
Financing is also being sought from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the EU's Phare project, which also financed the subway line's feasibility study, he added.
The government is expected to chip in 23 billion forints ($132 million), little less than a quarter of the costs, while the city of Budapest is expected to pick up 15.3 billion, Horn explained.
The 7.3 km long subway line will have 10 stops and is expected to carry 300,000 people a day, including up to 35,000 an hour during the rush hour, Mayor Demszky said.
Horn said he did not expect the subway project to be cancelled even if his government lost the general elections planned for next year.
"This country is full of intelligent people and any intelligent person could see that this subway line is needed," he said.
Some members of the opposition said earlier that Budapest would not need a new subway and that better streetcar lines would be able to handle the traffic.

Budapest started building its first subway line, the first in continental Europe, in 1894. The third and most recent line was started in the early 1970s and the last stretch was completed in 1990. ($ = 0.869 European Currency Unit ECUs) ($ = 174.5 Hungarian Forints)
